To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the nasal drops of rINF-βser were not efficacious in preventing natural colds in the fall of 1986 (P = 0.3) and 1987 (P = 1.0).
the use of recombinant IFN-β serine nasal drops did not reduce the incidence of rhinovirus-induced colds.
the administration of recombinant human interferon-β (rhIFN-β) by nasal drops is not an effective prophylactic treatment for rhinovirus infections.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the use of interferon as an antiviral agent for the prophylaxis and/or treatment of viral infections, including influenza, rhinovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus and herpes simplex virus.
the development and testing of recombinant human interferon (rIFN) for treatment and prophylaxis of viral infections.
the development of novel approaches to prevent or ameliorate the symptoms of the common cold.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
nasal drops of r-IFN-β are not effective in the prophylaxis of natural rhinivus colds.
rIFN- βser is ineffective for prophylaxis of natural colds.
rIFN- βser nasal drops do not have prophylactic efficacy against natural colds, but are safe.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of rIFN as prophylaxis against natural rhinoviruses is not effective.
the nasal administration of interferons for prophylaxis is not effective and is not toxic.
nasal administration of rIFN is not a viable option for prophylaxis of rhinovirus infections.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the nasal drops were not effective for prophylaxis of natural rhinivrus colds.
the lack of efficacy of rIFNβser in our study is not due to lack of bioavailability of rIFN in nasal drops, as the same formulation was effective in our previous studies of nasal rIFNα2b.
nasal drops of rINF-β are not effective in preventing natural rhinoviral colds.
